plan.contextChunk:
One classical example of the limitations of motion estimation from
images is the **aperture problem**. The aperture problem happens when
observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the
image frame, as shown in @fig-apperture_problem. If none of the
termination points are in view within the observation window (i.e., the
aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. Only the
component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

![Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what is visible within the observation window, appears as if the motion of the bar is in the direction perpendicular to the bar.](figures/optical_flow/apperture_problem.png){width="100%" #fig-apperture_problem}


:::{.column-margin}
The **Barber-pole illusion** is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

![](figures/optical_flow/barber_pole.png){width="40%"}
:::


### Representation of Optical Flow

We can model motion over time as a sequence of **dense optical flow**
images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at
time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. The problem with this formulation
is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory
followed by points in the scene over time. As time $t$ changes, the
location $(x,y)$ might correspond to different scene elements.

An alternative representation is to model motion as a **sparse set of
moving points** (tracks):
$$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This has the challenge

interactions.label: Rotation Speed
interactions.teaches: Altering the rotation speed and direction shows how horizontal spinning is mapped directly to a vertical sliding illusion, governed by the helix angle.

interactions.label: Isolate Aperture
interactions.teaches: Enabling the aperture mask hides the cylinder's top and bottom edges, demonstrating how losing boundary 'terminations' makes the vertical motion illusion absolute and unavoidable.

demo_steps.title: The Barber Pole Illusion
demo_steps.narration: Watch the cylinder spin horizontally. Because the stripes are diagonal helices, the visual system interprets this continuous horizontal rotation as a smooth downward vertical translation. The curved top arrow shows the true motion, while the vertical arrow shows what we perceive.

demo_steps.title: Hiding the Terminations
demo_steps.narration: Toggle the local aperture window. When the top and bottom circular caps of the cylinder are masked, your brain loses the physical 'terminations'—the points where the stripes end. Without these boundary cues, it is mathematically impossible to detect the horizontal spin, and the vertical illusion becomes complete.

demo_steps.title: Reversing the Flow
demo_steps.narration: Reverse the cylinder's rotation speed to -1.0. With the aperture active, the apparent vertical motion instantly flips to upward. Since a local edge detector can only measure motion perpendicular to the contour, the true horizontal component remains entirely hidden.

demo_steps.title: Resolving the Ambiguity
demo_steps.narration: Remove the aperture mask. By observing the top and bottom caps again, you can track the individual stripe endpoints sliding horizontally along the circular edges. This boundary information resolves the aperture ambiguity, allowing your visual system to perceive the true rotational motion.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Slightly elevated orthographic front view looking down at the top cap of the vertical cylinder to capture both the cylindrical depth and the flat horizontal rotation cue.

(2) The camera is positioned broadside to this vertical cylinder, looking directly at its front face, which means azimuth is 0 degrees. (3) The top circular cap of the cylinder is clearly visible as a foreshortened ellipse, showing that the camera is tilted downward from above, implying a positive elevation of approximately 15 degrees.

camera_view.view_notes: The cylinder is placed vertically at the center. The camera sits at an elevation of 15 degrees to match the elliptical perspective of the top cap shown in the textbook figure.

inline_constraints.camera: Align the initial camera projection so the ellipse eccentricity of the cylinder caps matches the source figure exactly.
